extracted.intended_audience: short-story readers, writers, literary-magazine editors, and the broader literary community interested in prizes and anthology selection
extracted.subtask_description: Announcements and historical/selection notes about which short stories are eligible for and chosen for the O. Henry Prize anthology, including evolving eligibility rules, publication-venue requirements, and the anthology's approach to translated work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original eligibility: U.S. authors only (1919)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first O. Henry Prize collection, published in 1919, 'ruled out all non-American writers.' Series editor Blanche Colton Williams noted that the terms omitted foreign authors from possible participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes Williams’s admission: 'According to the terms which omit foreign authors from possible participation in the prize, the work of Achmed Abdullah, Britten Austin, Elinor Mordaunt and others was in effect non-existent for the Committee.' This is presented as an instructive example of how eligibility rules shape a prize's scope and absences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-born authors eligible if they became U.S. citizens (mid‑20th century practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1955 student thesis on the O. Henry series mentioned that 'foreign-born authors were eligible if they became U.S. citizens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This records a historical eligibility nuance — not necessarily a current rule — showing how citizenship status affected eligibility at one point in the prize's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1990s expansion to include Canadian writers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1990s the prize was further opened to Canadian writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text suggests the practical motivation may have been to allow consideration of writers like Alice Munro; this signals that nationality-based exclusions were relaxed to include neighboring-country authors of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2003 eligibility expansion: all English-language writers appearing in North American publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the ninth series editor in 2003, the selection process was made 'wider-ranging' by 'allowing the consideration of all English-language writers appearing in North American publications regardless of citizenship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a formal change that broadened the prize’s remit; Publishers Weekly cited it as making the collection stronger. It ties eligibility to publication in North American outlets rather than to author citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-venue requirement (appearance in North American publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2003 revision emphasizes consideration of writers 'appearing in North American publications,' making venue of original appearance a central eligibility factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of eligible sources are implicit in the winners list (The New Yorker, Zoetrope, Freeman’s, The Paris Review, etc.), so prior publication in recognized North American magazines/journals is a practical eligibility/selection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of stories in translation and explicit credit to translators
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 volume includes ten remarkable stories in translation and credits translators (names and source languages appear alongside authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The announcement highlights translations from Bengali, Greek, Hebrew, Norwegian, Polish, Russian, and Spanish and lists translators by name, indicating that translated stories are eligible and translators are acknowledged as collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion to select brand-new work and curate across languages
rubrics_metrics.description: The guest editor for the 2022 volume, Valeria Luiselli, 'has selected a brand-new story by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, along with ten remarkable stories in translation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This signals that guest editors exercise curatorial judgment to include newly published or original pieces and to assemble a multilingual, cross-cultural list according to their editorial vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection values thematic variety and universal human appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of the twenty winning stories are 'predictably varied,' with many touching on 'the pandemic, love and loss,' and also including humor; 'their appeal is universally human.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The announcement frames thematic diversity and emotional/universal resonance as qualities represented among winners, implying such qualities are prized in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation quality framed as dynamic, living, and collaborative rather than 'tidy' literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Jenny Minton Quigley reports learning from Valeria Luiselli 'to dissolve my previous conception of “successful” (perhaps tidy) literary translation and open the borders of my thinking to the living, dynamic melding of languages undertaken by the translators here.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses an evaluative stance toward translated work: preference for translations that are inventive, fluid, and that 'meld' languages creatively rather than strictly literal renderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic principle: every story as a form of translation (thought → page → reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece asserts: 'For every story is a work of translation, if only from thought to page and then into the reader’s particular consciousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an aesthetic standard or lens for evaluation, this suggests judges/readers consider how effectively a story transfers inner thought into text and evokes a reader response — a broad criterion of literary success.
